title: Stage Capabilities: Upload Malware
summary: Upload Malware is the sub-technique of Stage Capabilities in which the adversary places malicious files on infrastructure so they are reachable later, either by the victim or by their own tooling. The uploaded content is broad: first stage payloads, droppers, loaders, full backdoors, post compromise utilities and, increasingly, backdoored legitimate software. Common destinations are adversary controlled or previously compromised servers, free code hosting and paste services, decentralised file storage where content is addressed by hash and takedown is difficult, cloud object storage and application platforms, and package or extension repositories used by developers. Two distinct delivery patterns follow. In the pull pattern the file waits on an internet reachable host and is retrieved from inside a victim network, often by a scripted download, which corresponds to later ingress tool transfer. In the supply pattern the file is published into a software store, package library or marketplace under a name and description that look trustworthy, and the victim installs it directly, frequently helped by typosquatting or by imitation of a popular package. Detection on the victim side comes from network and endpoint evidence: proxy, firewall and name resolution records for the download, file creation and execution correlations on hosts, and reputation or age data for the destination. Detection on the hosting side comes from provider abuse reports. Legitimate downloads share the same protocols, so the differentiators are the age and reputation of the host, the context of the request, and whether the resulting file is signed and expected.

beginner.definition: This sub-technique means putting malicious files somewhere they can be collected later. The attacker uploads the file to a server, an online storage service or a software store. Nothing is attacked at that moment.
beginner.whyItMatters: A prepared file turns a slow intrusion into a quick one, because the payload is already waiting. Public file and package services are hard to police, since they host mostly legitimate content. Attackers also plant backdoored versions of real software, so users install the malware themselves while believing they chose a normal tool.
howItWorks: The attacker chooses where the file will live, often a free or rented service.
They upload a payload, a downloader or a backdoored copy of real software.
They may also name it to look like a popular, trusted software product.
Victim machines then fetch the file quietly from inside the protected network.
Or users install it themselves from a software store or package library.
The file runs and gives the attacker their foothold or full toolset.
beginner.example: Imagine a stranger leaves a parcel in a public locker and mails the key to a hundred homes. Whoever opens the locker finds a package with a familiar brand name printed on it, so it looks safe. Nobody broke into the house to deliver it; the household fetched the parcel itself. Uploading malware works the same way. The dangerous item waits in plain sight on a shared public shelf, and the victim carries it inside, believing it came from somewhere trustworthy.
takeaways: Check the age and reputation of a host before trusting a download from it.
Monitor for new executable files created by browsers, scripts or office documents.
Use software sources you control and verify package names and publishers.

objectives: Explain why an adversary uploads malware before an intrusion begins.
Describe the difference between waiting payloads and backdoored software packages.
Identify network and endpoint records that reveal a malicious download.
Explain how typosquatting increases the chance a user installs a malicious file.
List the hosting types commonly used to stage malicious files.
Describe how this sub-technique relates to later tool transfer into a network.
